title: Acne prescribing & the combined pill
summary: The NICE NG198 12-week first-line combinations for acne, how to choose and counsel, antibiotic stewardship, and how combined oral contraceptives (including co-cyprindiol) fit in, with their VTE risk.

glance.think: Mild to moderate acne in a young adult, or a woman who also wants contraception or has hormonal acne.
glance.engine: Sebum, follicular plugging, *C. acnes* and inflammation; androgens drive sebum, so oestrogen-containing pills help.
glance.backbone: NG198: fixed topical combinations for 12 weeks; add an oral tetracycline for moderate–severe acne (never alone, never with a topical antibiotic); COC as an option, co-cyprindiol with a stop plan.
glance.never_miss: VTE risk with co-cyprindiol and other COCs (UKMEC); mood change; severe or scarring acne needing referral for isotretinoin.

what: A **19-year-old woman** with numerous **comedones and pustules** on the cheeks, jawline, perioral and nasolabial areas, unresponsive to cleansers. Periods are regular; she does not smoke or drink and has had no treatment yet.

list: Under **NICE NG198** definitions this is **mild-to-moderate acne**: any number of non-inflammatory lesions, **up to 34 inflammatory lesions and up to 2 nodules**. The lesion count, scarring or psychological impact could move her higher (course teaching: **psychological impact can raise the grade**).
Moderate-to-severe acne = **≥35 inflammatory lesions and/or ≥3 nodules**.

what: The **lower-face/jawline** distribution suggests an androgen ("hormonal") component. Regular cycles and no hirsutism make PCOS less likely, but still ask about hirsutism, weight, cycle changes and family history.

cause.h: How it works (acne pathophysiology → drug targets)

features.h: Clinical uses & where it fits — NICE NG198 first-line (12-week courses)

head: Severity
Offer one of (fixed combinations preferred)
rows: (a) **adapalene 0.1% + BPO 2.5%** gel (Epiduo); (b) **tretinoin 0.025% + clindamycin 1%** gel (Treclin); (c) **BPO 3–5% + clindamycin 1%** gel (Duac)
(a) **adapalene 0.3% + BPO 2.5%**; (b) tretinoin + clindamycin; (c) adapalene/BPO **+ oral lymecycline or doxycycline**; (d) **azelaic acid 15–20% + oral lymecycline/doxycycline**
BPO alone if the above are contraindicated; **COC** in women (with topicals); oral erythromycin/trimethoprim if tetracyclines are contraindicated (specialist advice)

list: **NG198 rules:** **No** topical or oral antibiotic **monotherapy**, and **no** topical + oral antibiotic together; Oral antibiotics **only with a topical retinoid or BPO**; Review at **12 weeks**; continue oral antibiotics beyond 6 months only in exceptional cases; Once clear, **maintain** with a topical retinoid ± BPO (fixed combination)
**Minocycline is not recommended** (lupus-like syndrome, autoimmune hepatitis, blue-grey pigmentation — see.

**Tetracyclines:** **Avoid in pregnancy, breastfeeding and under-12s.**; Doxycycline causes photosensitivity; take it upright with water and use sun protection; Doses: lymecycline 408 mg once daily; doxycycline 100 mg once daily (BNF — recheck)
Start **adapalene 0.1%/BPO 2.5% gel once daily at night**: it covers comedones and pustules with no antibiotic resistance.
Use tretinoin/clindamycin instead if BPO irritation or bleaching is a concern.
If she could become pregnant, NICE says to discuss that **topical retinoids should not be used in pregnancy**; **BPO/clindamycin** is the option without a retinoid.
Discuss her **contraceptive needs** at the same visit. If she wants contraception anyway, a COC can be added for its acne benefit.

**How it works:** oestrogen ↑ hepatic **SHBG** (less free testosterone) and suppresses **LH-driven ovarian androgen** production. Progestogens with anti-androgenic activity (cyproterone, drospirenone, dienogest) also **block the androgen receptor** and reduce 5α-reductase activity.

**Evidence:** Systematic reviews (Cochrane; Arowojolu 2012) show every COC studied reduces inflammatory and non-inflammatory lesions vs placebo, with **few consistent differences between progestogens**; A meta-analysis (Koo 2014, which you cited) found COCs **comparable to oral antibiotics by 6 months**; antibiotics work faster at 3 months
**In practice:** benefit takes **3–6 months**. COCs help inflammatory and comedonal acne and acne with hyperandrogenism (PCOS). They are not monotherapy for severe/nodular acne.

head: Option (UK)
Licensed for acne?
VTE risk per 10,000 women/year (FSRH/EMA)
Notes
rows: **Levonorgestrel / norethisterone / norgestimate** COC (e.g. Microgynon 30, Rigevidon, Cilest)
Reasonable first COC. The progestogen is androgenic in theory, but acne still improves via the oestrogen/SHBG effect
**Not in the UK** (anti-androgenic progestogen; Yaz-type pills have an acne indication in the US)
Also anti-mineralocorticoid — check potassium if on ACE-i/ARB/spironolactone
**Yes** — moderate–severe acne related to androgen sensitivity and/or hirsutism, **after topical therapy and oral antibiotics have failed**

MHRA 2013: use only for the licensed indication. It is also a contraceptive, so **do not combine with another hormonal contraceptive**. **Stop 3–4 cycles after the condition has resolved**; review regularly

list: **UKMEC (FSRH):** before any COC, check: BMI (≥35 = UKMEC 3) and BP; **migraine with aura (UKMEC 4)**; smoking at age ≥35; personal/family VTE, thrombophilia, immobility, postpartum, breastfeeding; liver disease, breast cancer, SLE with antiphospholipid antibodies, multiple CV risk factors

**Choice for this 19-year-old (if she wants hormonal contraception):** Start a **second-generation (levonorgestrel) COC** alongside the topical regimen; If acne is still a problem after 6 months, consider a third-generation or drospirenone pill; If acne is moderate–severe after topical + antibiotic failure, consider **co-cyprindiol**, with explicit VTE counselling and a stop date; NICE NG198 also says to **consider a COC in addition to topicals** in women, and not to use co-cyprindiol first-line

**Common question: breakthrough bleeding (BTB):** BTB is common in the first **3 cycles**; Check adherence, interacting drugs (enzyme inducers, St John's wort), vomiting/diarrhoea and smoking. **Exclude STI (chlamydia) and pregnancy**, and check cervical screening status; If it persists beyond 3 months, FSRH suggests trying a pill with a different progestogen or a higher oestrogen dose (30–35 micrograms); Tailored regimens (shortened or no pill-free interval) can increase early BTB; The observation that COCs cause less BTB than progestogen-only pills fits the FSRH data

**Spironolactone:** Off-label anti-androgen for persistent lower-face acne in women, typically **50–100 mg once daily** (up to 200 mg/day under specialist guidance); Needs **effective contraception** (risk of feminising a male fetus); Check U&E/potassium at baseline. Routine monitoring is often unnecessary in young healthy women — follow the local/specialist protocol; Side effects: menstrual irregularity, breast tenderness. Not used in men (gynaecomastia). In the UK it is usually started on **dermatology advice**

ol: **Skin care:** non-comedogenic products, a gentle pH-neutral cleanser twice daily, no picking or squeezing, oil-free sunscreen. Diet: no strong evidence for elimination diets (NICE).
**12-week fixed-combination topical** (as above), applied thinly to the whole affected area, not just the spots. If irritated, start on alternate nights or wash off after 1 h, then build up to daily.
**Discuss contraception**, if wanted, choose a COC using UKMEC (above).

**Review at 12 weeks:** Clear → stop antibiotics and **maintain** with a topical retinoid ± BPO; Improving → continue; Not improved → switch to another first-line option; Moderate–severe acne that has failed two courses, including an oral antibiotic → **refer for isotretinoin**
**Screen psychologically** (mood, self-harm) at every review — acne carries a high psychosocial burden.

list: **Acne fulminans → urgent referral, to be seen by a dermatologist within 24 hours** (the course "why?"): It is sudden, severe, ulcerating and haemorrhagic acne with **systemic features**: fever, malaise, arthralgia/bone pain (osteitis), raised inflammatory markers, leucocytosis; It is often triggered by **starting isotretinoin**, or by testosterone/anabolic steroids; It needs **oral corticosteroids** quickly (± pausing or reducing isotretinoin) to prevent severe scarring

**Refer to consultant dermatology for:** diagnostic uncertainty; **acne conglobata** or **nodulocystic acne**; mild–moderate acne not responding to two 12-week courses; moderate–severe acne not responding to a course that included an oral antibiotic; **scarring** or persistent PIH; **psychological distress** or a mental health disorder (also refer to mental health services for suicidal ideation); a suspected underlying endocrine disorder (PCOS with abnormal results → GP/endocrinology)

management: All NICE NG198 primary-care options (topicals, oral tetracyclines, and COCs within contraceptive competence) are within IP scope if you are competent. For **co-cyprindiol** and spironolactone in acne, follow the local formulary (often specialist advice). Isotretinoin: refer.
red_flags: Scarring, nodulocystic or rapidly worsening acne, or severe psychological distress: refer for isotretinoin assessment.
Calf swelling, chest pain or breathlessness on a combined pill: possible **VTE**, same-day assessment.
Co-cyprindiol: review at 3 months and stop once acne is controlled (MHRA).
pearls: "Twelve weeks before judging" — show her a calendar.
BPO **bleaches** towels, clothes and hair; retinoids **dry the skin and sensitise it to sun**.
On doxycycline: photosensitivity; oesophagitis (take upright with water); keep indigestion remedies and iron 2–3 h apart.
Women on a COC should know the **VTE warning symptoms** (calf pain/swelling, chest pain, breathlessness) and the **stroke symptoms**.
